title: All the stories that got the Mexico City paddock talking
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli touched down in Mexico earlier this week knowing that he stands on the brink of becoming Formula 1's youngest World Champion following a beautifully crafted victory last Sunday in Austin.

However, we didn't get to hear from him on Thursday in the Mexico City paddock, as the Mercedes racer was under the weather while recovering from a viral illness.

The 20-year-old stayed at the hotel after being given dispensation to miss his mandatory media duties at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez.

title: Why Tsolov has complicated Racing Bulls’ 2027 plans
excerpt:
Nikola Tsolov’s FP1 appearance for Racing Bulls in Mexico has put a further spotlight on the driver log jam in the Red Bull camp.

A frontrunner in F2 this year who has already logged F1 mileage through TPC running at Imola, Tsolov would ordinarily be primed for a Racing Bulls race seat in 2027.

The fact that in recent years Isack Hadjar, Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad all took part in FP1 sessions in Mexico indicates that it’s a rite of passage of sorts.

Indeed, a few weeks ago Racing Bulls Team Principal Alan Permane made it clear that there is a three-into-two scenario, confirming that Tsolov is very much in the frame.

The challenge for Red Bull’s management is that all three of the aforementioned drivers have performed superbly this season, and with Hadjar already confirmed alongside Max Verstappen at Red Bull there won’t be any changes at the senior team.

As the only rookie in the 2026 field, Lindblad has impressed, and from the outside it seems obvious that his job isn’t under threat. The Briton is relaxed about waiting for firm news.

“In the end, I'm just focused on my year and doing as best as I can,” said Lindblad. “I know that's the thing that's going to help me. Always, when performance is better, that helps.

“Honestly, it's not something I've wasted too much energy on. I've been part of Red Bull for a long time. I'm very much part of this family. So it's not something that I'm wasting much energy on.”

Lawson’s case isn’t so clear cut. At the start of this season most observers would have assumed that his long-term future was uncertain, and that he would be the obvious man to be dropped should Red Bull promote a youngster.

The New Zealander has made life more difficult for his bosses by not only regularly making Q3 and scoring points with Racing Bulls, but also by doing a solid job when he subbed for the injured Hadjar at the senior team. Dropping him now would be a harsh decision, to say the least.

“I just feel like it's been a very strong year for us,” he explained. “And especially the second half, things have been very, very strong. And trying to find that consistency in F1 is very, very hard, and it can go away from you very quickly.

“And with how many variables there are, it's obviously something that's always a factor, but for us, I think we've maximised really a lot this year, especially the second half.

“I'm not really sure much what more is expected, but I'm also not really sitting there thinking too much about the whole seat selection thing. A year ago I thought about it a lot, it was very much in my head. And you just drive worse – you just overthink things.

“So this year I feel like I haven't really thought about it much at all. And things have been strong, so I'm just trying to keep that keep that mindset up, trying to score as many points as I can in the season.”

Whatever happens, at least Lawson knows that he’s done the best job he can.

“That's the biggest thing as a driver,” he said. “You come away from a weekend sometimes, and even if you can't score points, I think the biggest thing is personally you want to be able to walk away and feel like you've done everything you can. And if you've done that, that's a satisfying feeling.

“Well it can be at least. It's more satisfying than if you don't, if you make a mistake or something like that. There are always things you can do better, and I'm sure looking over the year, there's a lot of things to tidy up.

“But overall, I feel like I've done a very strong season, and if I wasn't driving next year, I would feel like there wasn't much more that I could have done.”

Ultimately the key to his survival in a race seat could be those races he did for Red Bull. The traditional purpose of the Faenza team has always been to provide drivers to the senior outfit, and thus those who were no longer felt to be potential graduates have generally been dropped.

After the disappointment of 2025, Lawson seized his second chance at the Milton Keynes team.

“There was a lot of talk over the last 12 months after I left Red Bull that that maybe I wasn't a driver that could be good enough to drive in Red Bull, because of my start,” he said.

“And it's not really something I spoke too much about, but going back to the start of 2025, we did half a day in Jerez before the season, we had a compromised Bahrain test, and we had Melbourne where we missed P3 with an engine issue, and then China was a Sprint, and that was it.

“So versus this year, I feel like obviously having a lot more experience going into Red Bull this year, maybe if there's one thing I take from it, it's that at least I could show people that I can drive that car – or any car.”

title: Norris defends McLaren's progress ahead of Mexico City GP
excerpt:
Lando Norris has defended McLaren's 2026 development progress ahead of the Mexico City Grand Prix, and believes that the team have "had a pretty good year" after a tough start to the campaign.

The reigning World Champions suffered a slow start under the new ruleset, which included a double Did Not Start for Norris and McLaren team mate Oscar Piastri in China.

The team have made steady progress during the season, which culminated in Norris taking back-to-back wins in Hungary and the Netherlands, while a third victory in Madrid was denied due to an ill-timed Virtual Safety Car.

Although McLaren have fallen away from the front of the pack in recent races due to a difficult handling car, Norris is proud of the work achieved by the team so far.

"The car has been horrible and difficult to drive the whole season, just other teams have brought a lot more upgrades since and improved a lot more than what we have. Nothing more than that," said Norris during Thursday's media day in Mexico City.

"The team is still doing a good job, considering we were almost one and a half seconds off at the beginning of the year, one second off. The fact we even won almost three races was a pretty sizeable achievement in itself.

"So I think we’ve had a pretty good year, if we want to look at it from that perspective. Of course, we hold ourselves to a very high level, and we want to win everything we can.

"We started a long way behind at the beginning of the season, and we’ve done a good job to catch up. We’ve done better than the majority of other teams on the grid."

McLaren sit equal on points with Red Bull for P3 in the teams' standings, with two victories for Max Verstappen in recent races proving pivotal.

Piastri believes that staying ahead of Red Bull will prove difficult over the remainder of 2026 – with McLaren's focus already on 2027 – but remains hopeful.

"You just have to keep fighting. I think at the moment we know we’re not as competitive consistently as Red Bull are, but we’re adding performance to the car still, and there’s a lot of things that can happen," said Piastri.

"Reliability has been a big topic this year, so there’s still plenty of ways it can turn. But clearly, on pure performance, we need to make some steps forward, and we do still have some things coming to the car that’ll hopefully help with that.

"I think for us, it’s going to be a big challenge to stay ahead of Red Bull, but we’re always up for it."

title: ‘I don’t care’ about the Drivers’ Championship – Verstappen
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has insisted that he doesn’t “really care” about the fight for second place in the Drivers’ Championship and would rather focus on improving Red Bull’s challenger for 2027.

Recent results have demonstrated that the Milton Keynes-based outfit should never be written off – after a frustrating wait for victories, Verstappen marginally missed out in Azerbaijan before clinching consecutive wins in Malaysia and Singapore.

Their resurgence has propelled the Dutchman up the standings, where he now sits just six points behind George Russell in P2 and five adrift of third-placed Lewis Hamilton, while Red Bull are also level on points with McLaren.

Asked ahead of the Mexico City Grand Prix how important a strong finish in the Drivers’ Championship would be, Verstappen replied: “I don’t really care, because it’s only about first. So for me, I don’t care if I’m second or fifth.

“The only thing that we want to try and achieve is to be P3 in the Constructors’. That’s what I think the team wants, so that’s what we’ll try to do.”

Although Red Bull haven’t finished outside of the top three in the Teams’ Championship since 2015, Verstappen went on to explain that his biggest priority is ensuring that they begin next season with as strong a car as possible.

“[There are] still a lot of things that we want to change, and I hope that it will bring the car a bit more together,” he said. “That’s been the target already for a long time.

“Of course, we have improved a lot this year, but I think we are nowhere near satisfied enough, so there will still be a decent amount of changes for next year.”

Verstappen has won at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez five times in his career, but Red Bull’s struggles last time out in Austin – where he was unable to hold off Charles Leclerc for P2 – left him reluctant to expect another triumph.

“There were a few little issues that we found, which of course we were dealing with throughout the weekend,” he explained. “So it’s more about trying to learn from them, trying to fix them and trying to have a little bit more of a straightforward race.

“It’s not the same track, so it’s a very different scenario. It’s very hard to say. Of course, if we fix or know how to fix some of the things that we had in Austin, naturally your pace is better. It’s very simple.

“I had a bit of damage on my car. Some other bits were not where we wanted them to be, and from the engine side, it was not where we wanted it to be operating and performing, also in terms of horsepower.

“So a lot of little things that contribute to lap time lost. If you fix that, you naturally pick up pace. We know that if the car and engine are in better shape, then you should go faster. But here, there are so many different elements that come in that it’s very hard to predict whether suddenly you’re fighting for the win again or not.”

title: Hamilton outlines Ferrari's objectives for Mexico and beyond
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton believes ahead of the Mexico City Grand Prix this weekend that the "next five races are like test races", as the Briton pushes Ferrari to build a car capable of challenging for next year's titles.

Hamilton has enjoyed a strong sophomore season with the Scuderia, which has included victory at the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix as well as five further podiums.

Along with team mate Charles Leclerc, Hamilton has helped Ferrari up to second in the teams' standings, but with Red Bull closing quickly due primarily to Max Verstappen's two race wins in quick succession.

"I think these next five races are like test races," said Hamilton during Thursday's media day in Mexico City.

"Of course, we want to hold on to second in the Constructors’ Championship, but this is a time for us to really look at how the season has gone and continue working on and modifying our processes. I think we’ve already done that, and things have gotten to a better place.

"For me, I’m really focused right now on next year’s car, looking at the good things from this year and making sure we don’t lose them, but instead add to the chassis. And then, of course, in the background, I’m pushing as hard as I can to make sure we come with a power unit that can compete with Mercedes and Red Bull.

"Of course, I would love for us to finish on a high. I think the team deserves it, and everyone at the factory deserves it. We’ll be trying to get the absolute best and most out of every weekend."

Ferrari's 2026 challenger is considered one of the best on the grid through the corners, but has struggled to compete with the power units from Mercedes and Red Bull.

Hamilton believes this is the primary area that the team needs to focus on for the remainder of the season and ahead of 2027 if they are to challenge for the title.

"I think the engine is probably number one [priority]. We’ve got reliability, which is good. But if we were matching the power of the others, we would be fighting for the championship this year, which we know," said Hamilton.

"So rectifying that and closing the gap is important. I know everyone is working flat out at the factory to try to do that, and I trust them completely in that process. It won’t be easy, but it’s possible.

"And then with the car, you always want more downforce. You’re always looking for a wider window in which the car works better. At the moment, it’s quite narrow. When you get it right, it’s good, but it’s very narrow, and you’re in and out of it."

title: Leclerc assesses Ferrari's chances in Mexico City Grand Prix
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc believes Ferrari have the potential to win this weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix, but that they have "got to be perfect" in order to beat the likes of Mercedes and Red Bull.

Leclerc enters this weekend off the back of two runner-up finishes in Singapore and Austin, with hopes high that the Monegasque driver can go one step further in Mexico.

Despite the upturn in form after several races off the podium, Leclerc believes that both Mercedes and Red Bull still head into this weekend as favourites to take victory on Sunday.

"It's getting very close and we have good momentum with Singapore and Austin," said Leclerc during Thursday's media day in Mexico City.

"We have maximised our potential and I was relatively happy with the pace we've shown. Whether we are the favourites this weekend, I don't fully agree, I think Mercedes remain the favourites wherever we go.

"I think Red Bull are very strong recently, but if we maximise everything we have, then I hope it can be a great weekend for us.

"And as we've seen, I think the optimisation of our package is what eventually will make most difference. It's so difficult to put everything in the right window coming into Qualifying that if we manage to do so, then I think we've got a chance here, but for that we've got to be perfect."

Leclerc has only taken one victory so far this year, at the British Grand Prix back in July, and has yet to claim a pole position despite being regarded as one of Formula 1's strongest qualifiers.

Leclerc admitted that one of Ferrari's weakest points was optimising its package in Qualifying, especially with regards to putting the tyres in the ideal operating window.

"We've got a strong car but a car that is very sensitive whenever we get off the optimum window and we've paid a little bit the price recently in Q3, particularly when the track temperatures are going down," said Leclerc.

"We just struggle a bit more compared to the others to just keep everything in the right window. That's what happened in Austin unfortunately on the lap that counted the most and eventually we lost a front row because of that.

"It's a limitation we know and that we are focused on. Whether we have the solution short-term I'm not sure, but at least it's a point of focus and something that we'll make sure to try and get as right as possible coming Saturday here."

title: Russell opens up on relationship with Antonelli this season
excerpt:
George Russell has explained that while he still shares “a good relationship” with Kimi Antonelli, his team mate has simply “been at a higher level” over the course of the 2026 season.

A superb start to the year established Mercedes as clear frontrunners, but instead of the more experienced Russell enjoying the upper hand, it was the Italian who quickly built up a lead in the drivers’ standings.

Although no driver wants to be outperformed by their team mate, Russell admitted ahead of the Mexico City Grand Prix – where Antonelli will seal his maiden title as long as he finishes no lower than ninth – that they’ve not allowed the season to impact their working relationship.

“On a personal level, Kimi is obviously a great guy with lots of energy,” the Briton said. “We’ve had no reason this year not to continue a good relationship. I think a lot of these rivalries start because of on-track incidents or actions.

“The truth is, he’s been at a higher level than me this year so we’ve not really been in that situation too often – we’ve had one or two races. When it comes to the racing itself, we keep ourselves to ourselves and work with our individual engineers to try and get the most out of it.”

Despite issues with reliability and inconsistency, Russell has demonstrated that he is able to get the W17 into the perfect window and make the most of it – in Baku, for instance, he qualified on pole position by eight-tenths and held off Max Verstappen for victory.

But that memorable performance was followed by a retirement, P9 and P8 over three rounds, leaving him to question why there’s been such a gulf between his good and bad weekends.

“I think it’s definitely important for me to try and gain some consistency,” he said. “I’ve never had a season like this in my career where the performance has fluctuated so much.

“I know it’s in there because you can’t deliver performances like that in Baku if you’ve so-called ‘lost it’. We’re struggling to have a high hit rate. We don’t know why that is and as I said, I’ve never had it personally before in my career. I guess that’s the priority for me in these last few races.”

Asked whether he’s formulated a plan to beat Antonelli in 2027, with both drivers set to remain at Mercedes, Russell added: “I’ve been working with a sports psychologist for seven years now. That was through my most successful years in F1, and now of course, this has been the first year of real struggle.

“I think at least in the approach I have, we’re not boxers where you’re in a ring fighting directly against somebody else. We’re kind of fighting against ourselves, almost like a golfer in the way that a Qualifying lap, you’re there by yourself and it’s the work and preparation that you’ve done yourself that makes the difference to a good performance.

“I’m not directly looking at my number one competitor saying, ‘how am I going to beat this guy?’. It’s more that I’m looking at myself in the mirror thinking, ‘what do I need to do to not have these poor performances, and what were the feelings I had from myself and the car during the great performances to replicate that more often?’.”

title: Facts, stats and trivia ahead of the Mexico City Grand Prix
excerpt:
The 2026 Formula 1 season moves on to the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez this weekend for Round 19 on the calendar, the Mexico City Grand Prix.

Free Practice 1 and 2 will take place on Friday, October 30, followed by Free Practice 3 and Qualifying on Saturday, October 31, and the Grand Prix itself on Sunday, November 1.

Vital statistics

First Grand Prix – 1963

Track Length – 4.304km

Lap record – 1m 17.774s, Valtteri Bottas, Mercedes, 2021

Most pole positions – Jim Clark (4)

Most wins – Max Verstappen (5)

Trivia – The 20% air pressure reduction at 7,200ft AMSL (above mean sea level) means Mexico has taken over from Italy as the race with the highest top speeds. In the 2016 race, Valtteri Bottas set the fastest ever trap speed in F1 history (231.46mph) but Williams telemetry said his maximum speed reached 231.96mph before braking for Turn 1

Pole run to Turn 1 braking point – 830m

Overtakes completed in 2025 – 97

Safety Car probability – 60%*

Virtual Safety Car probability – 60%*

Pit stop time loss – 21.78 seconds

*From the last five races in Mexico

The driver's verdict

Jolyon Palmer, former Renault F1 driver: The Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez has a low downforce effect but, here in Mexico City, you run to the maximum due to the thin air. The car always feels low on grip and on the edge around here.

The big braking zones are tricky in the first half of the lap and it is always loose through the middle sector thanks to the aforementioned low downforce. You've got to work out how much kerb you can take early on; take too much and it can really unsettle the car.

The last sector is fiddly and it feels ridiculously slow through the stadium. The penultimate right-hander feels like it might be nothing, but it is arguably the easiest to crash on with low grip and the wall so close.

Grip level overall is very low and the car feels so clumsy at such a low speed. But the atmosphere around here in Mexico is great, which is such a buzz.

Everything to know about the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez

Last five GP polesitters in Mexico

2025 – Lando Norris (McLaren)

2024 – Carlos Sainz (Ferrari)

2023 – Charles Leclerc (Ferrari)

2022 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2021 – Valtteri Bottas (Mercedes)

Last five GP winners in Mexico

2025 – Lando Norris (McLaren)

2024 – Carlos Sainz (Ferrari)

2023 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2022 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2021 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

Tyre and strategy insight

"The Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez has traditionally been one of the least demanding circuits on tyres," reads Pirelli's weekend preview. "Its many low-speed corners and limited lateral loads tend to keep wear under control.

"At the same time, the thin air reduces the aerodynamic load generated by the cars, increasing tyre slip and making graining a factor to watch closely. With a new and smoother asphalt surface, this characteristic could play an even more significant role in shaping strategy.

"In Mexico, the track is often quite dirty during the first sessions, with grip improving significantly lap after lap. This year, that evolution could be even more pronounced given the extensive resurfacing work.

"From a strategic point of view, the circuit’s low severity and the behaviour of the three compounds on tracks with similar characteristics could favour a one-stop race. Tyre management to extend stints will nevertheless remain an important factor, particularly considering that the rear axle is the most heavily stressed.

"The difference between the various strategic options may depend more on the confidence a driver can extract from a particular compound than on any genuine tyre life limitation. As seen at several events this season, some teams may be more inclined towards the softer compounds in order to benefit from the additional grip available, while others may favour the consistency and stability offered by the hard.

"In any case, the soft could once again play a central role. The C5 has demonstrated strong characteristics on low-severity circuits and could prove an attractive option not only in qualifying but also in the race, broadening the range of strategic possibilities compared to previous seasons.

"Another aspect to monitor will be braking performance. The altitude reduces aerodynamic efficiency and can make the management of the heaviest braking zones more challenging. The long main straight leading into Turn 1 could increase the risk of lock-ups, especially during the early stages of the weekend when grip levels are still limited."

Current form

Kimi Antonelli scored his ninth win of the season last time out in Austin, resulting in his advantage at the top of the drivers’ standings growing to 123 points over Mercedes team mate George Russell.

This also means that the Italian could feasibly secure his maiden World Championship this weekend at the Mexico City Grand Prix. To do so, he needs to score just two more points – so a P9 finish is all he requires.

Should he fail to take any points, Antonelli could still clinch the title if neither Russell nor Lewis Hamilton win the race. A memorable few days might be in store, then, as the F1 paddock heads to the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez.

There is also a close fight brewing up behind, with Russell, Hamilton, Max Verstappen and Charles Leclerc all within 10 points of each other from P2 to P5 respectively in the standings.

Ferrari looked to have good pace in Austin, so can the Scuderia continue this form to put themselves ahead in the battle? Red Bull, meanwhile, have equalled McLaren on points and leapfrogged the papaya outfit to move up into third place of the Teams’ Championship.

In the midfield, Racing Bulls are pulling away fast in the scrap for P5 – having now amassed 102 points in comparison to 69 for sixth-placed Alpine – while Haas have so far kept Audi at bay in the P8 duel.

Iconic moment

The opening lap at the 2017 Mexican Grand Prix was eventful to say the least. Ferrari's Sebastian Vettel had managed to grab pole ahead of the Red Bull of Max Verstappen in P2 and title rival Lewis Hamilton in P3.

But as soon as the lights went out it was a young Verstappen who managed to force himself past Vettel at the second corner, allowing Hamilton himself to overtake the German. However, on the entry to the third corner Vettel clipped Verstappen's right rear tyre, and also subsequently came together with Hamilton's right rear.

Vettel would end up pitting for a new wing following that incident, while Hamilton limped back with a puncture – the two championship contenders now left in 19th and 20th respectively.

With Verstappen going on to seal the win, Vettel would battle back to fourth. However, Hamilton managed to haul his Mercedes up to ninth place and that was enough to secure the 2017 drivers' title.

title: Lewis Hamilton fires 'I'm built different' warning over key F1 question
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has insisted that F1 has "never had anyone like me" before, as he fielded a question about his potential participation in the African Grand Prix.

Earlier this month, as revealed by RacingNews365 and then formally announced by F1, the championship will return to the continent of Africa for the first time since 1993 with a grand prix in Rwanda sometime in the next decade.

F1 is hopeful that the event, due to be held at a purpose-built track near the capital, Kigali, will host its first race in the "early 2030s", with seven-time champion Hamilton declaring previously that he would not retire from F1 until the series had raced in Africa.

As per the "early 2030s" timeline, Hamilton will turn 45 in January 2030, with old rival Fernando Alonso currently at that age, with the Spanish racer going to turn 46 midway through the 2027 season.

Hamilton, who is statistically the greatest driver of all time with 106 wins, 104 poles and 208 podiums to go with his seven titles, would be nearing 500 grands prix by the end of the 2030 season, if he does not take a sabbatical and starts every race between now and then.

Questioned whether he could make it to the first race in Rwanda, Hamilton was in a punchy mood ahead of his 399th F1 race.

"I mean, firstly, you've never had anyone like me here in the 70 years, so I feel that I'm built differently," Hamilton declared to media, including RacingNews365.

"Of course, there are challenges up ahead that I can't foresee that come with age, but along this way, along this journey, there have been so many preconceived ideas about the fact that your reaction time drops off.

"Did you see my reaction in the last race? My reaction is faster than some of the youngest people here, so there are lots of tools that you can utilise to continue to keep yourself and your mind sharp.

"I guess as long as you're willing to sacrifice everything, which I am right now. I can't say in four years whether I want to continue to do what I'm doing, but I love what I'm doing still now.

"I'm still all in, and I will be for the foreseeable future. Whether or not I can compete at 44 with a 20-year-old, who knows? But at 41, I can compete with a 20-year-old, so time will tell whether I'm here in the 2030s; we'll see."

[Article continues below]

'Not outstaying my welcome'

However, Hamilton did also add that he would not "outstay my welcome" - but pointed to his remarkable turnaround in form from his dreadful 2025 season at Ferrari.

For the first time in his then 19-year F1 career, Hamilton failed to score a grand prix podium as he struggled with the final ground effect Ferrari - but bounced back to take a first podium for the Scuderia in the Chinese GP, and then added his name to the drivers who had won for the team with victory in Barcelona.

"I never want to overstay my welcome in the sense of still not having the performance," he added.

"I don't want to be walking, driving around with that really dropping off, that my reactions have dropped off, that my driving has dropped off, and my pace has dropped off, which everyone has seen last year, but I proved everyone wrong with that, and I'll continue to try to do so."

title: Max Verstappen responds to Daniel Ricciardo Le Mans tilt: 'He's a smart man'
excerpt:
Max Verstappen, Daniel Ricciardo and Sebastian Vettel racing together at Le Mans? Not as crazy as it sounds!

Max Verstappen has responded to Daniel Ricciardo's suggestion that the pair team up with Sebastian Vettel for a crack at the 24 Hours of Le Mans, joking that his former Red Bull team-mate knows exactly what he is doing.

Ricciardo, who retired from F1 last year and now serves as a Ford Racing ambassador, floated the idea of an all-star endurance line-up with Verstappen and Vettel on a recent podcast appearance.

Speaking to media, including RacingNews365, Verstappen gave the idea a cautious welcome.

"He's a smart man to choose me in the car," quipped the four-time F1 champion.

"But we have to see. It just depends on a lot of things. For me, if I want to do it, I want to do it properly with really good prep.

"At the moment, I cannot do that. I don't have the free time to dedicate to a Le Mans project with all the other things that I'm doing outside of Formula 1."

[Article continues below]

Verstappen - 'A conversation already had'

The topic is not a fresh one for Verstappen, who revealed the subject has already come up in previous discussions with Ricciardo.

"It's not new to me, of course," confirmed Verstappen. "Yeah, we have spoken.

"From my side or his side, I don't think we are the types who always need to share everything, right? We talk about a lot of things in the background.

"But I think he has said it himself. He doesn't see himself coming back for a whole season. But the one-offs are interesting, and why not?

"But again, if we do something like that, and he will agree for sure, it needs to be proper, for a chance to win.

"And for a chance to win against people who do it for a whole season, you need to be really well prepared, so you just need to find the right timing."

title: F1 remembers Hollywood legend with iconic Daniel Ricciardo moment
excerpt:
Formula 1 has paid tribute to Sir Patrick Stewart following confirmation of his death, sharing footage of the actor's memorable "shoey" with Daniel Ricciardo on the podium at the 2017 Canadian Grand Prix.

Stewart died on Wednesday at the age of 86 at his home in Los Angeles, with the news made public on Thursday through a statement from his family and spokesperson.

The Hollywood Reporter confirmed the cause as complications from Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia following a private illness.

The actor was best known for playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard across the Star Trek franchise and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men films, alongside a stage career spanning more than six decades that included extensive work with the Royal Shakespeare Company and acclaimed runs on Broadway and in the West End.

His F1 connection came at Circuit Gilles Villeneuve in June 2017, where Lewis Hamilton won from pole for Mercedes ahead of Valtteri Bottas and Ricciardo, who claimed third for Red Bull. Stewart conducted the official podium interviews that day and unexpectedly asked to take part in Ricciardo's celebratory ritual rather than being talked into it.

The moment quickly became one of the best and most widely shared celebrity crossovers in F1 podium history precisely because Stewart volunteered for a drink from the Australian's racing boot.

title: Liam Lawson addresses F1 future uncertainty as head-scratching continues
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has admitted he does not know what more he can do to secure his Racing Bulls seat for 2027, insisting he is refusing to fall into the same overthinking trap that derailed him a year ago.

The New Zealander heads into the Mexico City Grand Prix weekend still without clarity on his future, despite what he views as a career-best campaign at Racing Bulls.

Lawson picked up another points finish last time out at the United States Grand Prix, crossing the line in ninth after what team principal Alan Permane described as flawless execution.

Racing Bulls has yet to confirm its 2027 line-up, with the Faenza-based outfit weighing up three contenders for two seats. Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov is among those in contention and is set to make his grand prix weekend debut in first practice in Mexico, adding fresh intrigue to a decision Permane says is expected within weeks.

Speaking to select media, including RacingNews365, on media day in Mexico, Lawson reflected on a season he feels has answered any lingering questions about his form.

"I just feel like it's been a very strong year for us, and especially the second half, things have been very, very strong," he said.

"And trying to find that consistency in Formula 1 is very, very hard, and it can go away for me very quickly. And with how many variables there are, it's obviously something that's always a factor. But for us, I think we've maximised really a lot this year, especially the second half.

"So, yeah, I'm not really sure what more is expected, but I'm also not really sitting here thinking too much about the whole seat selection thing. Just because a year ago I thought about it a lot, it was very much in my head, and it just makes you overthink things.

"And so this year, I feel like I haven't really thought about it much at all, and things have been strong. So I'm just trying to keep that mindset up, trying to score as many points as I can and end the season with as many as I can."

Liam Lawson unsure what else he can do for F1 future

Lawson went on to explain the standard he holds himself to regardless of the result on a given weekend, especially in his current situation of possibly facing an F1 exit.

"That's the biggest thing as a driver. Like, you come away from a weekend, sometimes even if your car can't score points, I think the biggest thing is personally you want to be able to walk away and feel like you've done everything you can," he said.

"And if you've done that, that's a satisfying feeling. Well, it can be, at least. It's more satisfying than if you don't, if you make a mistake or something like that.

"So I do feel like this year there's always things you can do better, and I'm sure looking over the year there's a lot of things to tidy up. But overall, I feel like I've done a very strong season, and I think I would feel like if I wasn't driving next year, I would feel like there wasn't much more that I could have done."

title: Alex Albon 'doubles down' on Fernando Alonso counter: 'Hope our paths don't cross'
excerpt:
Alex Albon has doubled down on his insistence that he did nothing wrong in his collision with Fernando Alonso - that has sparked yet another gibe from the veteran.

On the opening lap in Austin last time out, Albon collided with the left-hand side of Alonso's car at the Turn 11 hairpin, destroying the aerodynamics and hobbling the Aston Martin.

After the race where both had finished outside of the points with the damage, Alonso claimed that the driving standards in the lower midfield were very low - with Albon initially brushing off his comments.

However, on media day in Mexico City, Alonso reiterated his comments and said that: "I'm not specific on the number of them, but I think we all know which ones we talk about and which ones felt hit by that comment.

"So that tells you everything. So I still feel the same. That was a mistake [by Albon]; it was not needed, and I still find it difficult to understand what the opportunity was that Alex saw in that moment."

Albon then doubled down on his belief that he had done nothing wrong in the collision, and said that he hoped he and Alonso would not clash this weekend in Mexico.

"Firstly, I would say that I hugely respect Fernando. I think he's a great driver, and I've looked up to him a lot growing up as a kid," Albon began when offered a response to Alonso's comments by media, including RacingNews365.

"I think we're all in our own little fight at the back. I don't think it's the level of the drivers as much. I would say the grid's the strongest it's been for a while, and obviously post-race comments are always a little bit more in the heat at the moment, so you can always say you can take it with a pinch of salt.

"I thought it was a good battle. I thought we had a good scrap, so clearly he didn't think the same thing, but it was a race-long battle. Even the incident itself, I thought, was very 50-50 in terms of where the cars were on track.

"I'll double down on what I said," Albon then said. "I have a huge respect for Fernando. I looked up to him a lot growing up as a kid; obviously it's not nice to hear those comments when you're racing someone that you look up to, but at the same time, I don't agree.

"It's as simple as that. I think the level is strong up and down the grid. I think 10-15 years ago, it wasn't. The back half of the grid wasn't the way it is now; we don't have pay drivers anymore, so it is what it is.

"Hopefully, we don't cross corners or cross paths in the race this weekend."

[Article continues below]

Drivers defend Albon

Other midfield drivers, including Pierre Gasly and Oliver Bearman, also defended Albon against Alonso's comments, declaring the level to be "super-high."

"I'm pleased I'm in the first half of the grid so I've made the cut myself," Gasly quipped.

"I mean, you've got to love Fernando for the statements he makes out there, and I have so much respect for the driver he is, and at the same time, he's very vocal.

"I haven't seen his race. I'm not too sure what he referred to, but I will say that the level on the grid is probably one of the highest, considering all the drivers we have now, from what I've seen [earlier in my career], and I've seen some wilder driving approaches when I joined, compared to what I see now.

Bearman declared Alonso's gibe to be "slightly harsh."

"I think that's a slightly harsh conclusion because I agree with Pierre that the level is very high on this current grid," he said.

"I think with the gaps that we face this year, you have to be very opportunistic at times, and that can end in disaster, as it did for me last week with Pierre and myself.

"So I wouldn't say it's a question of quality. It's a question of trying your very best and trying to make something happen, which is very challenging when the top eight positions are pretty much all filled by the top four teams."

title: How F1 title forecasts shift
excerpt:
An in-depth look at how F1 title forecasts can shift over the course of a season, especially when it gets to the end.

Kimi Antonelli's victory at the 2026 United States Grand Prix left the championship looking all but decided.

It was the Mercedes driver's ninth win of the season and moved him to 365 points, 123 clear of team-mate George Russell. Lewis Hamilton sits another point behind in his Ferrari.

Five grands prix remain, with 125 points available. Russell and Hamilton are still in contention mathematically, although either needs Antonelli to surrender almost his entire lead.

A title forecast had to reflect how unlikely that had become.

[Article continues below]

© XPB Images

A points lead means more as the calendar shrinks.

Antonelli went into the summer break 50 points ahead of Hamilton. Mercedes had started the new regulations strongly, but Ferrari and McLaren were winning races, too. With 12 grands prix left, there was time for the order to change.

By October 25, the gap had more than doubled, with fewer than half as many races left.

The title maths:

Russell trails Antonelli by 123 points.

Only 125 grand prix points remain.

Even five Russell wins will not suffice if Antonelli scores three more points.

[Article continues below]

Why forecasts and market prices can disagree

Championship forecasts are not all calculated in the same way. A statistical model can use recent race pace, past results and retirement rates to estimate how many points a driver is likely to collect. A prediction market reflects the prices at which people are willing to trade on an outcome. They can move quickly after a race.

Prediction markets also have a practical side that is separate from forecasting. A guide to a polymarket promo code, for example, explains account offers and participation conditions rather than how to assess a Formula 1 championship.

For anyone following a title market, that distinction matters: promotional terms describe access to the platform, while contract prices reflect trading activity. Neither replaces an assessment of the points gap, remaining races and each team's performance.

A driver whose title price improves after a fortunate safety car may not have become any quicker. Equally, a poor finish can conceal a strong car that was held back by an isolated incident.

[Article continues below]

© XPB Images

One difficult weekend can alter expectations

The Austin result gave forecasters more than another 25 points for Antonelli. He converted pole position into victory and finished over 13 seconds ahead of Charles Leclerc, while Russell came home eighth. The manner of the win gave Russell little encouragement.

A tighter race can change even faster. If a driver trails by 20 points, winning while the leader retires puts them five ahead. A convincing advantage in race pace would make that swing more significant than the points alone suggest.

Reliability can make an even bigger difference. One retirement costs a driver a weekend's points. Several failures suggest the car could lose more points later, and forecasts have to reflect that risk.

Qualifying can also flatter a car that struggles with tyre wear or race balance over a full grand prix.

[Article continues below]

Upgrades can overturn earlier form

The pace hierarchy rarely stays fixed across a season, particularly under a fresh set of technical regulations. Ferrari introduced significant developments during 2026, with Charles Leclerc urging an aggressive approach to upgrades as the team tried to close the gap.

An upgrade might work well at one circuit and offer less elsewhere. Race pace and tyre behaviour across several weekends provide better evidence of any sustained gain.

For a driver chasing the title, that improvement must also arrive early enough to turn into points.

[Article continues below]

© XPB Images

The remaining races determine what's possible

Under Formula 1's championship points system, a grand prix win is worth 25 points and second place earns 18. Sprint weekends can create additional scoring opportunities, although none remained after Austin in 2026.

A seven-point loss to the leader can be recovered with half a season remaining. Late in the year, a challenger may need victories as well as a succession of low scores from the driver ahead.

Russell's remaining chance after Austin depends on a succession of victories and unusually poor results from Antonelli. Given how consistently the Mercedes driver has scored, there is little reason to expect that combination to unfold.

Article provided by CBSsports

title: Fernando Alonso continues to brutally question ability of F1 rivals: 'I see things'
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso has not held back in his latest scathing remarks about some drivers on the current F1 grid.

Fernando Alonso has doubled down on his criticism of the drivers occupying the lower third of the grid, telling reporters at Mexico City Grand Prix media day that he stands by comments made after his clash with Alex Albon in Austin and insisting "I see things from the car that I cannot tell you."

The Aston Martin driver's frustration stems from a first-lap collision at Turn 11 during the United States Grand Prix, when Albon attempted to pass him on the inside and made contact, leaving Alonso's car with extensive floor and sidepod damage.

The incident went unpenalised by the stewards, prompting Alonso to brand the quality of drivers at the back of the grid as very low, a comment that drew a response from Albon, who insisted it was a normal racing incident given he had been squeezed from the outside by another car, and from Carlos Sainz, who pushed back on the broader characterisation.

Asked in Mexico whether F1 has an issue with driver quality in the lower third of the grid, Alonso told select media, including RacingNews365, that he was not fixing on a precise number.

"I don't know if it's the 1/3, because then I saw some reports trying to select eight drivers or seven drivers," said Alonso.

"I'm not specific on the number of them, but I think we all know which ones we talk about and which ones felt hit by that comment. So that tells you everything. So I still feel the same. That was a mistake [by Albon]; it was not needed, and I still find it difficult to understand what the opportunity was that Alex saw in that moment.

"But it's not only Austin. Unfortunately, it's that part of the race for the whole season, so I see things from the car that I cannot tell you."

Driver

Fernando Alonso

Spanish

14

Fernando Alonso surprised by 'happy to crash' rivals

The two-time champion was then asked whether he believed the standard at the back of the field had declined over the years, and rejected the idea that this was a new phenomenon.

"No, it's the same over the years," insisted the veteran. "Obviously, when you are at the back of the grid, the cars are more difficult to drive. They have less grip, so mistakes are coming more often because you don't have an environment that is under control.

"The car doesn't welcome you in a nice way. So you make more mistakes, but I don't feel that all the incidents on lap one, all the touches, all the front wings that fly around, all these kinds of things are necessary.

"Especially if you are fighting for nothing at the back of the grid, and there is the cost cap also adding to this problem. But if their teams are happy with the cost cap and breaking things every race, it's okay for them."

Alonso also addressed whether he felt the stewards should be taking a harder line on incidents further down the order, suggesting the responsibility lay elsewhere.

"It's not their job [the stewards'], unless there is something clearly unsafe," added Alonso. "So it's not part of the stewards' job.

"It's just whatever ambition those drivers have for the future: if they want to stay in Formula 1 for longer, if they want to have an opportunity in a bigger team, or if they are happy to crash."

title: Esteban Ocon reveals Lewis Hamilton conversation following Haas axe
excerpt:
Esteban Ocon is still in search of a new job after confirmation recently he will be leaving Haas at the end of the season.

Esteban Ocon has confirmed that Lewis Hamilton was kind enough to hold a conversation with him during the United States Grand Prix weekend following his recent axe by Haas.

Haas announced earlier this month that Ocon's contract would not be renewed after a two-season spell with the American team.

Owner Gene Haas and team principal Ayao Komatsu have instead opted to hand F3 champion Rafael Camara, who is also chasing this season's F2 title, an opportunity following a recent shootout at Portugal's Portimão circuit, where it is claimed his speed was impressive.

The decision means Ocon is in search of a new opportunity, preferably in F1, even as a third/test driver for a season to ensure he remains as high-profile in the paddock throughout 2027, in the hope of being back on the grid in 2028.

After mentioning that Lance Stroll was the only driver to have offered him any sympathy over his situation, a photo then emerged of the Frenchman chatting with Hamilton at the Circuit of the Americas.

Asked about the conversation, speaking to media, including RacingNews365, Ocon said: "Yeah, Lewis came to me in Austin.

"We chatted a little bit about the situation and how things went."

Suggested to Ocon that "it was nice", the seven-time F1 champion had made the effort, he replied: "For sure. Yeah, definitely."

[Article continues below]

Driver

Esteban Ocon

French

31

Ocon - 'A lot more tricky'

Ocon goes into this weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix as one of the 10 F1 drivers who will sit out first practice as part of the sport's rules in offering FP1 opportunities to rookies.

Ocon, who makes way for Japan's Ryo Hirakawa, does not see the lack of an FP1 as a major inconvenience for the remainder of the weekend.

"This track is not the hardest on the power unit normally," said Ocon. "With the simulator work that we've done, it doesn't translate as one of the very hard ones.

"We have quite a lot of freedom, quite a lot of deployment through the lap because there's a lot of braking, low drag. It's actually quite slippery in the air, and we are more limited with the speed threshold at high speed.

"It's obviously not ideal to miss FP1, but there is a chance that the track is very dirty in FP1.

"All in all, it's not a bad place to lose a session. It's quite late in the season, and we've got a good amount of learning now, and yes, there aren't that many corners.

"If you think of some other tracks where I could have given up another FP1, if you take Austin, for example, that would have been a lot more tricky."

title: Racing Bulls warned against F1 promotion: 'Both drivers would suffer'
excerpt:
Former IndyCar driver James Hinchcliffe has warned Racing Bulls that it will hurt the development of its drivers in 2027 if it opts to drop Liam Lawson.

Lawson is still awaiting word on whether he will be retained by the team next year as the squad weighs up its options.

It is anticipated that Arvid Lindblad will keep his drive at the squad after a positive rookie campaign, but who will drive alongside him remains unknown.

While Lawson is a candidate, so too is Nikola Tsolov, who is currently in contention for the F2 drivers' championship.

But Hinchcliffe has stated that having such an inexperienced line-up will have a negative impact on how much both can grow within F1.

"I was a rookie in IndyCar, I had a very experienced teammate, a decade, maybe 11 years already under his belt in Oriol Servia," Hinchcliffe told the F1 Nation podcast.

"I can tell you that, having worked with younger drivers later in my career, if I had a one, two, three-year driver as my team-mate that first year, my development in my rookie season would have been nowhere near as close.

"So for sure, Lindblad has benefited from Lawson because he's driving like somebody much more experienced and with much more tenure in the series than he currently has.

"Remember, he [Lawson] still has not yet done a full season of F1 with the same team from start to finish. He's had to bounce around a little bit there.

"Putting a rookie in beside Lindblad stunts his development, and then for Tsolov, you're learning off a driver with one year of experience.

"Both drivers, I think, suffer in that situation."

Not re-signing Lawson would be 'absolute madness'

Lawson has enjoyed a strong campaign so far with Racing Bulls and is on course to finish ninth in the drivers' standings, the leading driver outside of the top four teams.

He has bagged points at 13 of the 18 rounds staged so far and impressed on his return to Red Bull in the mid-season when Isack Hadjar suffered an injury.

Hinchcliffe insisted Lawson's performances more than warrant a retention for 2027.

"It blows me away that they haven't already," he said. "We spoke to him on the post-race show on F1TV, and we posed that question to him.

"His reaction was pretty genuine. He's like, 'dude, I don't know'. You can tell, he's kind of exasperated at this point too.

"It's not one of those, 'Oh yeah, I don't know. We'll see', clearly knowing it's already a done deal.

"I genuinely don't think he's been officially told. Not re-signing him would be absolute madness.

"I joked on the show, I said, 'Well, at this point, you should hold out because if you keep scoring points like this, you can get your base salary up a little bit higher.'"

title: Honda explain challenge facing every F1 team in Mexico as key absence felt
excerpt:
Honda has detailed the challenge facing every F1 team in the Mexico City Grand Prix, as the new power units are run at high altitude for the first time.

At 2,285m above sea level, the air density at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez is around 25% lower than at sea level, meaning the turbo must spin faster to ensure it can provide the air the engine requires to perform.

Previously, this function was aided by the MGU-H, which helped to reduce turbo lag - the delay between the demand for power and the turbo actually providing it.

Now, with the MGU-H removed from the 2026-spec engines, the turbo will receive no support and have to work considerably harder to fulfil the same duties as in 2025.

Analysing the situation, Honda's chief engineer Shintaro Orihara explained the challenge in detail.

"This is the first time running in Mexico, and last year, we had the MGU-H, so we had some support from the MGU-H, but this year, we don't have it," Orihara told media, including RacingNews365.

"That is quite challenging, and for example, in idle, we had MGU-H support to get inner boost pressure, but this year, we don't have any support in idle.

"I think not only Honda, but all power unit manufacturers will struggle with power with these power units, but it is not only power.

"In Mexico, turbocharger speed is quite high to get airflow, and then we may need to check, but we may have some restrictions on engine function in the worst case.

"We have done a lot of dyno testing, and we believe there is almost no impact on energy operations, but we need to check in practice."

Orihara was then questioned about why, if higher turbo RPM was being recorded, turbo lag could be an issue.

"The turbocharger has some limitations in terms of operating speed," he said.

"And if we hit the operating speed, we can provide a good solution, and at the moment, we don't have any concerns."

[Article continues below]

Honda's turbocharger

One issue Honda has struggled with since introducing its second ADUO boost in Spain and Azerbaijan has been turbo lag.

However, following a positive weekend last time out in the United States, Orihara was positive that knowledge had been gained to reduce the effect of it.

"In Austin, we worked with countermeasures for turbo lag, and we have confirmed the effect of the turbo lag, and it was quite positive for us coming here," he said.

"So I think that is a positive, and also in Sakura, they are still working hard to optimise power, and in Sakura, they are still working on how to improve turbo lag.

"So it is quite important to see how our turbo behaves in free practice, but I am sure this is not only for Honda, but other manufacturers.

"We have done dyno testing in Sakura to simulate Mexico conditions, so we have some idea of what will happen, but without any running at high altitude physically for the first time, it will be quite interesting to see how our turbocharger behaves."

title: Second F1 driver ruled out of Mexico media day as illness confirmed
excerpt:
Valtteri Bottas has been withdrawn from Thursday's media day in Mexico City after falling ill, Cadillac has confirmed.

The Finn, who is enduring a difficult season with the American outfit, had been due to face reporters ahead of the Mexico City Grand Prix but was instead sent back to his hotel to rest.

Bottas is the second driver on the grid to miss Mexico media day, after Mercedes confirmed Kimi Antonelli had also been ruled out with a viral illness.

Cadillac has stressed that Bottas's absence is purely precautionary and does not currently put his participation in the rest of the weekend in doubt.

In a team statement, Cadillac said: "Cadillac Formula 1 Team can confirm that Valtteri Bottas will unfortunately be unable to attend today's media day in Mexico City as he is unwell."

"The team has taken the decision to allow him a day of rest, to support his recovery."

"This is a precautionary measure and does not currently affect his participation in the remainder of the race weekend. We will continue to monitor the situation and provide updates if necessary."

Under FIA sporting procedures, teams must request a medical dispensation to excuse a driver from mandatory media duties, with any return to track action requiring clearance from team doctors or, if necessary, the FIA Medical Delegate.

It remains to be seen whether either Bottas or Antonelli will need that formal clearance before taking part in first practice on Friday.

title: Kimi Antonelli misses Mexico City media day as 'viral illness' revealed
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli enters the weekend he will likely be crowned world champion very much under the weather.

Kimi Antonelli will miss Thursday's media day in Mexico City as he continues to recover from a viral illness, Mercedes has confirmed.

The 20-year-old was due to face the written press and broadcasters alongside his rivals ahead of the Mexico City Grand Prix, but the Brackley-based squad has secured dispensation from the FIA to excuse him from his mandatory duties.

Antonelli is expected to be fit to take part in the rest of the weekend's track action, with Mercedes stressing that the decision is purely precautionary as he builds up his strength before Friday's practice sessions at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez.

Mercedes' confirmation of Antonelli's absence read: "Kimi is feeling under the weather today as he recovers from a viral illness.

"As a precaution, the FIA have excused him from his mandatory media duties to give him the chance to rest ahead of the weekend.

"We expect him to be back tomorrow."

Kimi Antonelli faces challenging weekend

Viral illnesses typically bring fever, fatigue and muscle aches, and recovery over a race weekend usually hinges on rest, hydration and a reduced workload to guard against the cognitive fatigue that comes with prolonged exposure to cockpit heat.

Under FIA regulations, teams must formally notify the governing body's media delegate when a driver is unable to fulfil press commitments through illness, which shields Antonelli from any penalty for his absence on Thursday.

Should any doubt remain over his fitness closer to the race, the FIA's medical delegate retains the authority to check he is fully fit before he is cleared to get back in the car.

For now, Mercedes' message is one of cautious optimism, with the Italian due back in the paddock on Friday.

It is a significant weekend for Antonelli, who will be crowned world champion in the Mexican capital should he finished ninth or better if George Russell wins and 10th or better if Lewis Hamilton wins.

title: Daniel Ricciardo opens door to racing return with Max Verstappen reunion
excerpt:
Daniel Ricciardo has not taken part in a professional race event since exiting F1 towards the end of the 2024 season.

Daniel Ricciardo has suggested he would be open to the possibility of reuniting with Max Verstappen with an entry at the 24 Hours of Le Mans.

Ricciardo has not raced since he exited the F1 grid following the 2024 Singapore Grand Prix.

The Australian has spent much of the time out of the public view and involving himself in activities he did not have time for while navigating the F1 schedule.

During his time in F1, he spent three seasons alongside Max Verstappen at Red Bull before departing the squad at the end of 2018.

Although Ricciardo suggested his full-time racing days are over, he hinted that he could be tempted by an entry that doesn't require year-round commitment.

"The thought of just doing a full championship or something still doesn't really sound that exciting," Ricciardo told the Beyond the Grid podcast.

"Probably a one-off like Le Mans. Maybe there's one of those scenarios that could perk me up.

"To take the helmet off and have a better view of racing than what I had after Singapore and all that, that would probably be a nicer form of closure."

When asked to name his dream line-up for Le Mans, Ricciardo added: "I don't want to put pressure on him, but obviously Max is a name that would be high on the list.

"We'll see. If it's right and things align, and it feels right and I'm there for the right reasons, maybe I won't say never."

It was then put to Ricciardo that he could reunite with another former team-mate in Sebastian Vettel in a Le Mans line-up, to which the Australian replied: "Well, butter my butt and call me a biscuit. That'd be cool."

[Article continues below]

Driver

Daniel Ricciardo

Australian

Ricciardo keen to avoid 'ego' decision over Le Mans

The 24 Hours of Le Mans is one of the most prestigious events in motorsport, and currently forms part of the World Endurance Championship.

Verstappen himself has voiced a desire to take part in the race in the future, having already started to dip his toes into endurance competition with outings at the Nurburgring and Portimao.

While Ricciardo feels the temptation to also get involved, he asserted that he will only do so if it feels it is a right fit.

"Do I need to open the box again? That's why I haven't rushed into making a decision on anything," he said.

"Again, I want to make sure I'm not doing it for ego or for some fairy tale ending, it has to be because it's right inside me, and I really want to do it, it's not to please others.

"There is a part of me which would love to do it for all the people that cared and supported and loved me over the years, and also hated the way it ended.

"Would I go to Le Mans just to go and compete, and just be happy to be there, or would I go there to try and win?

"As much as I want to say, 'oh, just be happy soaking in the experience'.

"Once the helmet is on, it's different. I won't hold everything to it; if I did it, it wouldn't change the way I feel.

"The result wouldn't dictate how things happen moving forward. But I can't deny that I would want to go and do it properly, and that's maybe something I need to understand as well.

"'Is my heart in it, am I doing it for the right reasons?' And also, if you share a car with others, you don't want to let them down either."

title: Ferrari value nears jaw-dropping $20 billion as crucial report released
excerpt:
Ferrari's brand value has grown by more than 14 percent to reach $17.7 billion, according to Interbrand's best global brands 2026 report.

The Italian manufacturer has climbed three places in the influential annual ranking to number 51, placing it among the study's 'Top Risers' for the year.

The report also confirms Ferrari's position as the world's most valuable Italian global brand. Brand strength remains high too, with a brand strength score of 85, while the brand's influence on consumer choices, measured by Interbrand's role of brand score, stands at 73 percent.

Interbrand's best global brands study is described as the world's longest-running and most influential analysis of its kind.

Ferrari has pointed to the results as confirmation of its broader approach across what it describes as its three "souls": racing, sports cars and lifestyle.

"These significant results for 2026 and the sustained upward trend are a further confirmation of Ferrari's overall strategy across its three souls: racing, sports cars and lifestyle," read Interbrand's findings, as presented by Ferrari.

"They also demonstrate its ability to expand coherently and credibly into new arenas, from selected luxury and lifestyle categories to racing projects such as offshore sailing."

Ferrari's F1 operation heads into the final stretch of the 2026 campaign with Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc, with the team looking for a strong Mexico City Grand Prix this weekend.

title: Rising British star handed Andretti Formula E role after impressive year
excerpt:
Callum Voisin has been confirmed as Andretti Formula E's official development driver, stepping into the role ahead of the 2026/27 ABB FIA Formula E world championship season.

The British-Swiss driver's appointment follows his outing with the American squad at the official rookie test in Madrid earlier this year.

He will now become a key part of Andretti's simulator programme and race preparation, supporting Jake Dennis and Felipe Drugovich as the series moves into its Gen4 era.

Much of that work will happen away from the track. Voisin will work closely with Andretti's engineers to build understanding ahead of each race weekend, with his simulator duties set to prove valuable as the team adapts to a new generation of Formula E machinery.

Voisin arrives on the back of a standout season in Porsche Carrera Cup GB, where he sealed the 2026 title with Rosland Gold by Century Motorsport with two races to spare, finishing the campaign with nine victories.

That form adds to a racing background spanning single-seaters, sports cars and endurance racing. Having won the 2023 GB3 Championship with Rodin Carlin, Voisin progressed to Formula 3, where he claimed a feature race win from pole position at Spa-Francorchamps in 2024.

He has also combined his British Porsche campaign with appearances in Porsche Carrera Cup Italia, and competed in the Asian Le Mans Series with High Class Racing.

For Voisin, the role offers a chance to deepen his relationship with Andretti after a brief introduction earlier this year.

"I'm really pleased to be joining Andretti Formula E as official development driver," said Voisin.

"Working with the team at the rookie test gave me a great introduction to how everyone operates, so it's exciting to be building on that relationship. There's a lot to learn with Gen4 and I'm looking forward to supporting the team prepare for each race."

Andretti outline 'foundation to build on' with Callum Voisin hiring

Voisin's first taste of Formula E machinery came at the 2025 official rookie test in Berlin with Cupra Kiro, where he finished fifth overall, before joining Andretti for the 2026 rookie test at Circuito del Jarama in Madrid in March.

Team principal Campbell Hobson, who took up the role earlier this year as Roger Griffiths moved into an advisory position, views the appointment as a way to strengthen the team's preparation while continuing Voisin's development.

"We're pleased to welcome Callum into a more permanent role with Andretti Formula E," said Hobson.

"His work in the simulator will be an important part of our race preparation, supporting our engineers and both drivers as we build our understanding of Gen4.

"Having already worked together at the rookie test earlier this year, there's a foundation to build on and his success across different categories demonstrates his ability to adapt to new challenges."
